examples.knowledge_point: Utilizing the Evenness Property of the Secant Function
examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the graph of $y = \sec{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13934039/assets/fbf6ef1ca91f998ab4dc2dda1890ffc8a713f2eeff19e5569351b2466256d63a.png)

From the graph, we note the following:

- The period of $\sec{x}$ is $2\pi.$

- Our graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis. This means that $\sec{x}$ is an *even* function, and we have

$$
\sec(-x) = \sec{x}.
$$

Let's now evaluate our expression:

- Firstly, using the periodicity of $\sec{x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}sec⁡(-x-14\pi ) & =sec⁡(-x-2\pi \cdot 7) \\  & =sec⁡(-x).\end{aligned}
$$

- Secondly, using the evenness of $\sec{x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}sec⁡(-x) & =sec⁡x \\  & =-\frac{11}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\sec(-x - 14\pi) = -\dfrac{11}{6}.$

feedback.worked_solution:
The period of $y=sec⁡x$ is $2\pi .$ Therefore, for integer $n$ we have

$$
sec⁡x=sec⁡(x+2n\pi ).
$$

Substituting $n=10$ into the right-hand-side of the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sec⁡x=sec⁡(x+2\cdot 10\cdot \pi )=sec⁡(x+20\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $sec⁡x=2\sqrt{5},$ then $sec⁡(x+20\pi )=2\sqrt{5}.$

Finally, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}sec⁡(x+20\pi )-3 & =\sqrt{5}(2\sqrt{5})-3 \\  & =2(5)-3 \\  & =10-3 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$
